newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court hears plea against war crimes trial.
newsitem.headline: French court hears plea against war crimes trial.

text.p: France's supreme court heard on Thursday a last-ditch attempt by former cabinet minister Maurice Papon to avoid trial for World War Two crimes against humanity.
The 87-year-old former official of the collaborationist wartime Vichy government, accused of sending 1,690 Jews to Nazi death camps in 1942-44, had said he would attend the hearing.

But he was absent when the Cour de Cassation, France's supreme court for this type of case, began hearing his lawyers' plea behind closed doors. Justice sources said the court would hand down its ruling next Thursday.

An appeals court ruled last September that Papon should be tried for crimes against humanity, only the second Frenchman -- and probably the last -- to be sent for trial on such charges arising from World War Two.

A lower-ranking collaborator, former militia officer Paul Touvier, was jailed for life in 1994 and died in prison last year aged 81. Another accused collaborator, Rene Bousquet, was shot dead by a publicity-hungry failed writer in 1993 before he could stand trial.

Papon is accused of ordering the deportation of the Jews, including 223 children, when he was secretary-general of the wartime regional administration in Bordeaux, southwest France. Most were later gassed at the Auschwitz death camp.
Papon rose to be Paris police chief in the 1960s and a Gaullist budget minister in the 1970s before his World War Two role was exposed.

"Staging a trial of the (wartime) Vichy regime against a genuine Resistance member is a monumental historical absurdity," argued Jacques Bore, one of Papon's lawyers. Papon says he joined the French Resistance against the Nazis in 1943.
"The Vichy state never had an administration aimed at perpetrating crimes against humanity. Its anti-Jewish legislation was deplorable but not genocidal," Bore added.
Arnaud Lyon-Caen, a lawyer for the civil plaintiffs, retorted that the persecution of the Jews was the result of Vichy's policy of collaboration and its anti-Semitic, xenophobic stance.

The Bordeaux court, after 15 years of procedural battle, went further than prosecutors had sought, sending Papon to a jury trial in an assize court on charges of being an accomplice to the kidnapping and murder of deportees in 10 convoys to Nazi death camps.
Prosecutors had linked him to just four convoys which left Drancy, near Paris, for the death camps in 1942 and 1944, while victims' relatives held him responsible for six more trains.
The court also approved charges that Papon was an accomplice to arbitrary arrests, the arrest of minors under 15 years old, inhuman acts and attempted illegal arrests.
The prosecutor had argued that Papon must have known about Hitler's "final solution" -- the Nazi extermination of the Jews of Europe -- although he had no evidence to back this.

Papon's lawyers countered that Papon never followed Nazi ideology and had only obeyed orders. Papon enjoyed a meteoric post-war career until the satirical weekly Le Canard Enchaine revealed his wartime activities in 1981.
Since then, he has benefited from delaying tactics by a succession of governments and justice officials keen to avoid a trial.
